1.why: All screens use a clean sans-serif typeface with ample letter spacing, line height, and whitespace around text blocks.

2.why: No italics or all-caps appear; instructional text is broken into short sentences inside light info boxes rather than dense paragraphs.

3.why: Content is presented in a single narrow centered card with large tap targets and stacked fields that fit a mobile viewport without horizontal scrolling.

4.why: Instructions such as “MFA is required before high-value payments can be authorised” and “We sent a six-digit verification code…” are brief and use everyday words.

5.why: An explicit mock verification code (037020) and a sample phone number are shown, though the six-digit TOTP field itself lacks a format example.

6.why: Primary instructions remain short; only the evaluation-behaviour note under the secret is a longer block, and it is not required to proceed.

7.why: The long authenticator secret is rendered as selectable plain text in a box, allowing copy-and-paste rather than manual re-typing.

8.why: No QR code or any alternative to typing the manual setup secret is offered on the authenticator enrolment screen.

9.why: Standard email and telephone input fields are present (likely to accept browser autofill), but no password-manager or autocomplete attributes are visible for the OTP fields.

10.why: Each screen has a clear bold heading stating the current step and a single prominent blue button for the primary action.

11.why: Every step presents only one main call-to-action (Continue, Verify identity, Set up authenticator, Activate authenticator); secondary actions are visually de-emphasised.

12.why: The sole error message (“Verification could not be completed.”) does not explain what happened next or how to proceed, and no success confirmation text is shown after steps.

13.why: The form can be resubmitted after an error, yet no control is provided to re-request an expired verification code or to reveal/hide the secret.

14.why: The error “Verification could not be completed.” names a generic problem but supplies no recovery guidance and does not tell the user what to change.

15.why: A five-minute expiry is explicitly imposed on the SMS verification code, contradicting the claim of no time limit, although five minutes is moderately generous.
